note: EDITORIAL (round 14, DATA_DECISIONS section 73): the tree of life through time. Each node is a lineage: originMa is when it split from its sister lineage (originKind divergence/estimate, from molecular clocks such as TimeTree 5) or its oldest accepted fossil (originKind fossil); ageRange is [older, younger] where the literature disagrees; extinct lineages carry extinctMa. A child is never older than its parent. Topology follows current phylogenomics (two-domain tree with Eukaryotes inside Asgard archaea; ctenophores sister to other animals; turtles with archosaurs; whales inside Artiodactyla). merges record endosymbiosis: a lineage joining another. Edit this file and bump version; never edit data/biology/evolution/tree.json.

bands.name: Great Oxidation Event
bands.summary: Oxygen from cyanobacteria accumulated in the atmosphere for the first time, beginning about 2.43 billion years ago and completing by about 2.06 billion years ago.

bands.name: End-Ordovician extinction
bands.summary: Glaciation and sea-level fall wiped out about 85 percent of marine species in two pulses; the second of the five great mass extinctions by severity.

bands.name: Late Devonian extinction
bands.summary: A drawn-out crisis of reef collapse and ocean anoxia (the Kellwasser and Hangenberg events) that ended the placoderms and most armoured jawless fishes.

bands.name: End-Permian extinction
bands.summary: The Great Dying: Siberian volcanism drove the loss of about 90 percent of marine and 70 percent of land species within about 60,000 years, 251.9 million years ago.

bands.name: End-Triassic extinction
bands.summary: Volcanism as the Atlantic opened killed off the large pseudosuchian archosaurs and many marine groups, clearing the way for dinosaurs.

bands.name: End-Cretaceous extinction
bands.summary: The Chicxulub asteroid impact, with Deccan volcanism, ended the non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, ammonites and marine reptiles 66 million years ago.

nodes.name: Last universal common ancestor
nodes.summary: The population of cells from which all living things descend: already a complex organism with DNA, ribosomes and hundreds of genes, dated by molecular clocks to roughly 4.2-3.8 billion years ago, within a few hundred million years of Earth's formation.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.summary: One of the two primary domains of life; the oldest widely accepted fossils of any organism are 3.4-3.5-billion-year-old stromatolites and microfossils from Western Australia that were almost certainly built by bacteria.

nodes.name: Cyanobacteria
nodes.summary: The inventors of oxygen-producing photosynthesis; their rise is the only plausible driver of the Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago, though the lineage itself is probably several hundred million years older.

nodes.name: Proteobacteria
nodes.summary: A vast, metabolically diverse phylum of Gram-negative bacteria that includes E. coli, nitrogen fixers, purple photosynthesisers and the ancestors of mitochondria; its age is a molecular-clock estimate, as bacterial fossils rarely preserve diagnostic shapes.

nodes.name: Alphaproteobacteria
nodes.summary: The class that includes Rickettsia and the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium, and from whose ancestors the mitochondrion descends: every eukaryotic cell carries a domesticated alphaproteobacterium.

nodes.name: Gammaproteobacteria (E. coli, Vibrio)
nodes.summary: The best-studied bacterial class, home to Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Vibrio and Pseudomonas; a molecular-clock estimate places its origin in the late Archean to early Proterozoic.

nodes.name: Firmicutes (Bacillus, Clostridium)
nodes.summary: Thick-walled bacteria including the spore-forming Bacillus and Clostridium and the lactic-acid bacteria of yoghurt and the gut; among the deepest-branching bacterial groups by most genomic analyses.

nodes.name: Actinobacteria (Streptomyces)
nodes.summary: Filamentous soil bacteria that produce most natural antibiotics (Streptomyces) and include Mycobacterium, the agent of tuberculosis; dated only by molecular clocks.

nodes.name: Spirochaetes
nodes.summary: Corkscrew-shaped bacteria that swim with internal flagella; the group includes the agents of syphilis and Lyme disease and symbionts of termite guts, and its deep age is a clock estimate.

nodes.name: Archaea
nodes.summary: The second primary domain: single cells without nuclei but with membranes, enzymes and gene-expression machinery that differ from bacteria; carbon-isotope evidence for methane-producing archaea reaches back 3.46 billion years.

nodes.name: Methanogens and halophiles
nodes.summary: Archaea that make methane in oxygen-free mud, guts and seafloor sediments, and their salt-loving relatives; methanogenesis is among the oldest metabolisms with a geochemical trace.

nodes.name: Thermophilic archaea (TACK)
nodes.summary: Heat- and acid-loving archaea of hot springs and hydrothermal vents, with the ammonia-oxidising Nitrososphaeria of the open ocean; part of the TACK superphylum that sits closest to the eukaryote host lineage.

nodes.name: Asgard archaea
nodes.summary: Discovered in 2015 from deep-sea sediment DNA, these archaea carry proteins once thought unique to eukaryotes; the eukaryote host cell arose from within or beside this group, which is why Eukaryotes branch here in a two-domain tree.

nodes.name: Eukaryotes
nodes.summary: Cells with a nucleus and mitochondria, formed when an archaeal host took in an alphaproteobacterium that became the mitochondrion; the earliest fossils with eukaryote-grade features are about 1.65 billion years old, and clocks put the common ancestor at roughly 1.8-2.0 billion years.

merges.label: Mitochondrial endosymbiosis
merges.note: An alphaproteobacterium taken up by the archaeal host became the mitochondrion; every eukaryote descends from this merger.

nodes.name: Euglenids and trypanosomes
nodes.summary: Flagellates such as the photosynthetic Euglena and the parasitic trypanosomes that cause sleeping sickness; a deep eukaryote lineage dated only by molecular clocks.

nodes.name: Plants, algae and SAR
nodes.summary: The eukaryote supergroup that unites the plant lineage (Archaeplastida) with the SAR clade of diatoms, dinoflagellates and foraminifera; its name means 'diverse'.

nodes.name: Plant lineage (Archaeplastida)
nodes.summary: Red algae, green algae and land plants, the lineage that gained photosynthesis when an ancestor engulfed a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast; the fossil red alga Bangiomorpha (1.05 billion years) sets the minimum age.

merges.label: Plastid endosymbiosis
merges.note: A cyanobacterium engulfed by an early Archaeplastida cell became the chloroplast; plants and algae photosynthesise with its descendants.

nodes.name: Red algae
nodes.summary: Mostly marine seaweeds and coralline algae; Bangiomorpha pubescens, a 1.047-billion-year-old fossil from Arctic Canada, is the oldest taxonomically resolved eukaryote and a red alga.

nodes.name: Green plants
nodes.summary: Green algae and land plants, with chlorophyll b and starch stored inside the chloroplast; the billion-year-old seaweed Proterocladus is the oldest green-plant fossil.

nodes.name: Green algae (Chlorophyta)
nodes.summary: Single-celled and seaweed green algae such as Chlamydomonas, Volvox and sea lettuce; a one-billion-year-old multicellular form from North China shows the group was already diversifying then.

nodes.name: Charophyte algae and land plants
nodes.summary: Freshwater green algae such as Chara and Spirogyra together with all land plants, which arose from among them; clocks place the split from other green algae around a billion years ago.

nodes.name: Charophyte algae (stoneworts)
nodes.summary: Freshwater algae that are the closest living relatives of land plants; stoneworts build calcified stems that fossilise, but the earliest charophyte fossils are Silurian, far younger than the clock age.

nodes.name: Land plants
nodes.summary: Plants that live on land and protect their embryos: molecular clocks place the origin in the middle Cambrian to early Ordovician, and the oldest fossil spores are about 470 million years old.

nodes.name: Mosses, liverworts and hornworts
nodes.summary: Small plants without true vascular tissue that still need films of water to reproduce; the oldest land-plant fossils, Ordovician cryptospores, were most likely shed by liverwort-grade plants.

nodes.name: Vascular plants
nodes.summary: Plants with lignified water-conducting tissue, which let them grow tall; Cooksonia, a finger-high Silurian plant from about 433 million years ago, is the oldest widely accepted vascular plant.

nodes.name: Clubmosses and quillworts
nodes.summary: The oldest surviving vascular-plant lineage: Baragwanathia from the late Silurian of Australia is a clubmoss, and giant tree-sized lycophytes later formed much of the Carboniferous coal.

nodes.name: Ferns and seed plants
nodes.summary: The lineage with true leaves, uniting ferns and horsetails with all seed plants; it split from the clubmosses in the Silurian or earliest Devonian.

nodes.name: Ferns and horsetails
nodes.summary: Spore-bearing plants with large leaves and a free-living fertilised stage; the earliest fern-like plants are early Devonian, and most modern fern families arose only after flowering plants took over the forests.

nodes.name: Seed plants
nodes.summary: Plants that package the embryo with food in a seed, freeing reproduction from water; Runcaria from Belgium (about 385 million years) is a seed precursor and the first true seeds appear in the latest Devonian.

nodes.name: Conifers
nodes.summary: Cone-bearing trees such as pines, firs and redwoods; the oldest conifer fossils are late Carboniferous, and the group dominated the world's forests through the Mesozoic.

nodes.name: Cycads
nodes.summary: Palm-like seed plants with large cones, now about 350 species in the tropics; Crossozamia from the early Permian of China is the oldest unambiguous cycad.

nodes.name: Ginkgo
nodes.summary: A lineage of broad-leaved seed plants reduced today to a single species, Ginkgo biloba, whose fan-shaped leaves are recognisable in Permian rocks.

nodes.name: Flowering plants
nodes.summary: Plants with flowers and fruit, now some 300,000 species; unambiguous angiosperm pollen appears about 135 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous, while molecular clocks suggest a Triassic origin that the fossil record has yet to confirm.

nodes.name: Monocots (grasses, lilies, palms)
nodes.summary: Flowering plants with a single seed leaf and parallel-veined leaves: grasses, orchids, lilies and palms; the group split from other angiosperms early in the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Eudicots (oaks, roses, daisies)
nodes.summary: About three-quarters of all flowering plants, defined by pollen with three furrows; such tricolpate pollen first appears about 125 million years ago.

nodes.name: SAR (stramenopiles, alveolates, rhizarians)
nodes.summary: A supergroup of mostly single-celled eukaryotes recognised only from genomes in 2007: brown algae and diatoms, ciliates and dinoflagellates, and the shell-building foraminifera.

nodes.name: Diatoms
nodes.summary: Glass-shelled algae that fix about a fifth of the planet's carbon; the oldest unambiguous diatom fossils are Early Jurassic, though their silica cells may have evolved earlier.

nodes.name: Brown algae (kelp)
nodes.summary: Kelps and rockweeds, the largest protists, whose forests shelter coastal ecosystems; they evolved multicellularity independently of plants and animals, around the Jurassic by clock estimates.

nodes.name: Dinoflagellates
nodes.summary: Whip-swimming plankton that light the sea with bioluminescence and power coral reefs as symbionts; their resting cysts are common fossils from the Triassic onward.

nodes.name: Foraminifera
nodes.summary: Amoeba-like cells that build chambered shells; their fossils date the Cambrian and later rocks so reliably that they are the workhorses of oil-well stratigraphy.

nodes.name: Amoebozoans, fungi and animals
nodes.summary: The eukaryote supergroup that contains amoebae, fungi and animals; its ancestor was most likely a flagellated cell that fed by engulfing bacteria.

nodes.name: Amoebae and slime moulds
nodes.summary: Amoeba proteus, the social slime mould Dictyostelium and relatives, which move by flowing pseudopods; dated by molecular clocks, with vase-shaped Tonian microfossils as a possible early record.

nodes.name: Fungi and animals
nodes.summary: The group named for the single rear flagellum of its swimming cells, as in human sperm and chytrid spores; fungi and animals are each other's closest relatives.

nodes.name: Fungi
nodes.summary: Absorptive feeders with chitin walls, from yeasts to mushrooms; Ourasphaira from Arctic Canada (1.01-0.89 billion years) carries chitin and may be the oldest fungus, with unambiguous fungi known from the Ordovician.

nodes.name: Chytrids
nodes.summary: Mostly aquatic fungi whose spores still swim with a flagellum, a trait the rest of the fungi lost on land; one species is the pathogen devastating frogs worldwide.

nodes.name: Pin moulds and relatives
nodes.summary: Fast-growing moulds such as Rhizopus on bread, together with the Glomeromycotina that partner with the roots of most land plants, a symbiosis as old as plants on land.

nodes.name: Higher fungi
nodes.summary: Fungi whose cells carry two unfused nuclei for part of the life cycle: the sac fungi and the club fungi, together the great majority of described species.

nodes.name: Sac fungi (yeasts, morels, Penicillium)
nodes.summary: The largest fungal phylum: brewer's yeast, Penicillium, morels and truffles, and most lichen fungi; their spores form inside sac-like asci.

nodes.name: Club fungi (mushrooms, rusts)
nodes.summary: Mushrooms, puffballs, bracket fungi and the rust and smut parasites of crops; their spores form on club-shaped basidia, and the oldest mushroom fossils are Cretaceous amber.

nodes.name: Choanoflagellates
nodes.summary: Single cells with a collar of tentacles around a flagellum, nearly identical to the feeding cells of sponges; the closest living relatives of animals.

nodes.name: Animals
nodes.summary: Multicellular eukaryotes that eat other organisms; molecular clocks place the common ancestor of living animals at roughly 850-650 million years ago, a hundred million years or more before the first unambiguous animal fossils of the Ediacaran.

nodes.name: Comb jellies
nodes.summary: Gelatinous swimmers that row with bands of cilia; chromosome-scale gene linkages published in 2023 support them, rather than sponges, as the sister group of all other animals.

nodes.name: Sponges
nodes.summary: Filter-feeders without tissues or nerves, pumping water through their bodies; molecular sponge biomarkers are reported from 635-million-year-old rocks but remain debated.

nodes.name: Jellyfish, corals and anemones
nodes.summary: Radially symmetrical animals armed with stinging cells; Haootia, a 560-million-year-old Ediacaran fossil with muscle fibres, is the oldest widely accepted cnidarian.

nodes.name: Jellyfish
nodes.summary: Cnidarians whose life cycle includes a free-swimming medusa; soft-bodied jellyfish impressions are known from the Cambrian, though the lineage is surely older.

nodes.name: Corals and sea anemones
nodes.summary: Polyps that never form a medusa; reef-building stony corals appear in the Triassic, after the Palaeozoic reefs of the extinct tabulate and rugose corals.

nodes.name: Bilaterians
nodes.summary: Animals with a head end and mirror-image left and right sides, which is almost every familiar animal; Kimberella and the first burrows, about 555 million years old, are the earliest fossil evidence.

nodes.name: Protostomes
nodes.summary: The bilaterian branch whose embryos form the mouth first; it holds the great majority of animal species, from molluscs and worms to all arthropods.

nodes.name: Molluscs, annelids and relatives
nodes.summary: Protostomes with a trochophore larva or a lophophore feeding crown: molluscs, segmented worms, brachiopods and bryozoans, all abundant in the Cambrian explosion.

nodes.name: Molluscs
nodes.summary: Soft-bodied animals with a muscular foot and, usually, a shell; shelly molluscs are among the first Cambrian fossils and Kimberella (555 million years) may be a stem mollusc.

nodes.name: Snails and slugs
nodes.summary: The largest mollusc class, on land, in fresh water and in the sea; tiny coiled shells such as Aldanella appear in the early Cambrian.

nodes.name: Clams, mussels and oysters
nodes.summary: Two-shelled filter-feeders; Fordilla and Pojetaia from the early Cambrian are the oldest bivalves, and the class flourished after the end-Permian extinction.

nodes.name: Cephalopods
nodes.summary: Molluscs with arms and a jet; Plectronoceras from the late Cambrian of China is the oldest, a small shelled form ancestral to nautiloids, ammonoids and the modern octopus and squid.

nodes.name: Ammonites
nodes.summary: Coiled-shelled cephalopods that swam the seas for 340 million years and are the classic fossils of the Mesozoic; the last of them died with the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

nodes.name: Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish
nodes.summary: Cephalopods that internalised or lost the shell and gained the most complex invertebrate brains; Carboniferous fossils such as Pohlsepia are the earliest candidates.

nodes.name: Segmented worms
nodes.summary: Earthworms, leeches and the bristle worms of the sea; bristle worms are well preserved in the Cambrian Sirius Passet and Burgess Shale faunas.

nodes.name: Brachiopods
nodes.summary: Two-shelled filter-feeders unrelated to clams, hugely abundant in Palaeozoic seas and reduced to a few hundred species today; shells appear in the early Cambrian.

nodes.name: Moulting animals
nodes.summary: Animals that grow by shedding a cuticle: roundworms, velvet worms, tardigrades and the arthropods, which together make up most animal species.

nodes.name: Roundworms
nodes.summary: Unsegmented worms that may be the most numerous animals on Earth, from soil dwellers to the lab model C. elegans; soft-bodied, they have a sparse fossil record and are dated mostly by clocks.

nodes.name: Tardigrades
nodes.summary: Eight-legged 'water bears' half a millimetre long that survive freezing, vacuum and radiation in a dried state; relatives of the Cambrian lobopodians.

nodes.name: Arthropods
nodes.summary: Jointed-legged animals with an exoskeleton, by far the most diverse animal phylum; trace fossils from about 537 million years ago and trilobites from 521 million years ago mark their arrival.

nodes.name: Trilobites
nodes.summary: Three-lobed armoured arthropods that were the signature animals of the Palaeozoic seas, with over 20,000 species, until the last survivors died in the end-Permian extinction.

nodes.name: Chelicerates
nodes.summary: Arthropods with pincer-like mouthparts and no antennae: spiders, scorpions, mites, horseshoe crabs and the extinct sea scorpions; Sanctacaris from the Burgess Shale is an early member.

nodes.name: Spiders, scorpions and mites
nodes.summary: Eight-legged terrestrial chelicerates; Silurian scorpions and the 414-million-year-old trigonotarbid Palaeotarbus are among the first animals on land.

nodes.name: Horseshoe crabs
nodes.summary: Marine chelicerates whose body plan has barely changed since Lunataspis in the Late Ordovician, 445 million years ago; four species survive.

nodes.name: Mandibulates
nodes.summary: Arthropods with jaws (mandibles): the myriapods, crustaceans and insects; Cambrian fossils such as Yicaris already show crustacean features.

nodes.name: Centipedes and millipedes
nodes.summary: Many-legged land arthropods; Kampecaris and Pneumodesmus from the Silurian are among the oldest air-breathing animals known.

nodes.name: Crustaceans and insects
nodes.summary: Genomes show that insects arose from within the crustaceans; together they form Pancrustacea, the most species-rich group of animals.

nodes.name: Crustaceans
nodes.summary: Mostly aquatic arthropods with two pairs of antennae: crabs, shrimps, barnacles, copepods and krill; Yicaris from the early Cambrian of China is a well-preserved early crustacean.

nodes.name: Crabs, lobsters and shrimps
nodes.summary: Ten-legged crustaceans; Palaeopalaemon from the Late Devonian is the oldest decapod, and true crabs appear in the Jurassic.

nodes.name: Insects
nodes.summary: Six-legged arthropods, over a million described species; Rhyniognatha from about 400 million years ago has insect-like jaws, and a phylogenomic clock places the insect common ancestor in the Early Ordovician.

nodes.name: Dragonflies and damselflies
nodes.summary: Aerial predators with two pairs of independently beating wings; their Carboniferous relatives the griffinflies had wingspans up to 70 centimetres.

nodes.name: Beetles
nodes.summary: Insects whose forewings hardened into protective cases, the largest order of animals with some 400,000 species; the oldest beetles come from the early Permian.

nodes.name: Wasps, bees and ants
nodes.summary: Membrane-winged insects, from sawflies to the social bees and ants; the oldest are Triassic sawflies about 245 million years old, and ants appear in Cretaceous amber about 100 million years ago.

nodes.name: Flies and mosquitoes
nodes.summary: Two-winged insects whose hindwings became balancing organs; Grauvogelia from the Middle Triassic is the oldest fly, and mosquitoes appear in the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Butterflies and moths
nodes.summary: Scale-winged insects; wing scales from the Triassic-Jurassic boundary of Germany (about 201 million years) are the oldest trace, predating flowering plants by some 70 million years.

nodes.name: Deuterostomes
nodes.summary: The bilaterian branch whose embryos form the anus first: starfish and their relatives, acorn worms, and the chordates including ourselves.

nodes.name: Starfish, urchins and sea cucumbers
nodes.summary: Five-fold symmetrical marine animals with calcite skeletons and a water-vascular system; Helicoplacus and the early echinoderms appear in the Cambrian about 525 million years ago.

nodes.name: Acorn worms
nodes.summary: Burrowing marine worms and the colonial pterobranchs, whose extinct relatives the graptolites are key Palaeozoic index fossils.

nodes.name: Chordates
nodes.summary: Animals with a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord and gill slits at some stage; Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia from the 518-million-year-old Chengjiang biota are the oldest.

nodes.name: Lancelets
nodes.summary: Small fish-shaped filter feeders that keep the chordate body plan at its simplest; Pikaia from the Burgess Shale (505 million years) is a likely relative.

nodes.name: Sea squirts
nodes.summary: Sessile filter-feeders whose tadpole larvae reveal them as chordates and, by genomics, the closest living relatives of vertebrates; Shankouclava from the Cambrian may be the earliest.

nodes.name: Vertebrates
nodes.summary: Chordates with a skull and a backbone of vertebrae; the oldest, Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, are jawless fish from the early Cambrian of China.

nodes.name: Lampreys and hagfish
nodes.summary: The last living jawless vertebrates, with round sucking mouths; molecular data unite them as a clade, and Priscomyzon, a 360-million-year-old lamprey, shows how little they have changed.

nodes.name: Armoured jawless fishes
nodes.summary: Jawless fish encased in bony armour, such as Sacabambaspis and the Devonian Cephalaspis; they flourished for a hundred million years and vanished at the end of the Devonian.

nodes.name: Jawed vertebrates
nodes.summary: Vertebrates with jaws, which evolved from the front gill arches; complete jawed fishes from 439 million years ago in Chongqing, China, and Ordovician scales push the origin toward 450 million years.

nodes.name: Placoderms
nodes.summary: Armoured jawed fishes including the six-metre Dunkleosteus; they dominated Devonian seas and died out entirely at its end.

nodes.name: Sharks, rays and chimaeras
nodes.summary: Jawed fishes with cartilage skeletons and tooth-like scales; the oldest shark-like fishes are early Silurian, and the group has survived every mass extinction since.

nodes.name: Sharks
nodes.summary: Modern sharks (neoselachians) diversified in the Jurassic, though shark-like fishes go back to the Devonian; about 500 living species range from dwarf lanternsharks to the whale shark.

nodes.name: Rays and skates
nodes.summary: Flattened sharks' relatives with wing-like fins; the oldest ray fossils are Early Jurassic.

nodes.name: Bony fishes
nodes.summary: Jawed vertebrates with bony skeletons, which includes every land vertebrate; Guiyu from the late Silurian of China, 425 million years old, is the oldest articulated bony fish.

nodes.name: Ray-finned fishes
nodes.summary: Fishes with fins supported by bony rays: more than half of all living vertebrates; scales of Andreolepis from the Silurian are the first record.

nodes.name: Teleosts
nodes.summary: The modern ray-finned fishes, from herring and salmon to tuna and seahorses, some 30,000 species; Triassic fossils and clock estimates place their origin between the Carboniferous and the Triassic.

nodes.name: Lobe-finned fishes and tetrapods
nodes.summary: Bony fishes with fleshy, limb-like fins, the lineage that walked onto land; Guiyu and Psarolepis from the Silurian are stem sarcopterygians.

nodes.name: Coelacanths
nodes.summary: Deep-water fishes thought extinct since the Cretaceous until one was caught off South Africa in 1938; the lineage reaches back to the Early Devonian.

nodes.name: Lungfishes
nodes.summary: Air-breathing fishes of Africa, South America and Australia, the closest living relatives of land vertebrates; Diabolepis from the Early Devonian is the earliest.

nodes.name: Tetrapods (four-limbed vertebrates)
nodes.summary: Vertebrates with limbs and digits; Tiktaalik (375 million years), Acanthostega and Ichthyostega record the fish-to-tetrapod transition, and trackways from Poland may push it to 395 million years.

nodes.name: Amphibians
nodes.summary: Tetrapods that typically lay eggs in water and breathe partly through the skin; the living groups (frogs, salamanders, caecilians) share a common ancestor whose age is debated between the Carboniferous and the Permian.

nodes.name: Temnospondyls
nodes.summary: Large flat-headed amphibians such as Eryops and the crocodile-like Mastodonsaurus; the group ran from the Carboniferous to the Early Cretaceous, and living amphibians may descend from among them.

nodes.name: Frogs and toads
nodes.summary: Tailless jumping amphibians; Triadobatrachus from the Early Triassic of Madagascar, about 250 million years old, is the oldest frog-like fossil.

nodes.name: Salamanders and newts
nodes.summary: Tailed amphibians, many able to regrow limbs; Triassurus from the Triassic of Kyrgyzstan is the earliest, with crown salamanders well known from the Jurassic.

nodes.name: Caecilians
nodes.summary: Limbless burrowing amphibians of the tropics; Eocaecilia from the Early Jurassic still had tiny legs.

nodes.name: Amniotes
nodes.summary: Tetrapods whose eggs carry their own water in an amnion, freeing them from breeding in ponds: reptiles, birds and mammals; Hylonomus from Nova Scotia, about 312 million years old, is the oldest unquestioned amniote.

nodes.name: Synapsids
nodes.summary: The amniote branch with a single opening behind each eye, leading to mammals; Archaeothyris from the Late Carboniferous is the oldest known.

nodes.name: Pelycosaur-grade synapsids (Dimetrodon)
nodes.summary: Sprawling early synapsids such as the sail-backed Dimetrodon, top predators of the early Permian; they gave way to the therapsids by the middle Permian.

nodes.name: Therapsids
nodes.summary: More upright, more active synapsids including the dicynodonts and gorgonopsians; they dominated the late Permian, were decimated at its end, and one line became mammals.

nodes.name: Cynodonts
nodes.summary: Dog-toothed therapsids with differentiated teeth and a secondary palate; Thrinaxodon and its kin survived the end-Permian catastrophe and gave rise to mammals in the Triassic.

nodes.name: Mammals
nodes.summary: Warm-blooded, fur-covered synapsids that nurse their young; shrew-sized Late Triassic forms such as Brasilodon and Morganucodon, 225-205 million years old, are the first mammaliaforms.

nodes.name: Monotremes (platypus, echidnas)
nodes.summary: Egg-laying mammals of Australia and New Guinea; molecular clocks put their split from other living mammals in the Jurassic, and Teinolophos (120 million years) is the oldest fossil.

nodes.name: Marsupials and placentals
nodes.summary: Mammals that give birth to live young; the marsupial and placental lines had already separated by 160 million years ago, when Juramaia lived.

nodes.name: Marsupials
nodes.summary: Mammals whose young complete development in a pouch: kangaroos, koalas, opossums; the lineage is as old as Juramaia's, with Sinodelphys (125 million years) a possible early member.

nodes.name: Placental mammals
nodes.summary: Mammals that nourish the fetus through a placenta; Juramaia from 160-million-year-old Jurassic rocks of China is the oldest eutherian, and the living orders radiated around the end of the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Armadillos, sloths and anteaters
nodes.summary: A South American radiation with extra joints in the spine; the extinct giant ground sloths and glyptodonts were among the largest Ice Age mammals.

nodes.name: Afrotheres
nodes.summary: Mammals of African origin recognised only through genomics: elephants, manatees, aardvarks, hyraxes, elephant shrews and tenrecs.

nodes.name: Elephants and relatives
nodes.summary: Trunked mammals from the fox-sized Eritherium of 60 million years ago through mastodons and mammoths to the three living elephants.

nodes.name: Northern placentals
nodes.summary: The placental supergroup that arose in the northern continents and includes most familiar mammals, from bats and whales to rodents and primates.

nodes.name: Laurasiatheres
nodes.summary: Named for the ancient northern continent of Laurasia: shrews, hedgehogs, bats, carnivores, hoofed mammals and whales.

nodes.name: Bats
nodes.summary: The only flying mammals, about 1,400 species; Onychonycteris from Wyoming, 52 million years old, could fly but had not yet evolved echolocation.

nodes.name: Carnivorans (cats, dogs, bears, seals)
nodes.summary: Mammals with shearing carnassial teeth; the civet-like miacids of the Eocene are their stem, and the cat and dog branches had separated by about 42 million years ago.

nodes.name: Even-toed ungulates and whales
nodes.summary: Hoofed mammals bearing weight on two toes together with the whales, which genomics and fossils show evolved from among them, closest to the hippos.

nodes.name: Cattle, deer, pigs, camels and hippos
nodes.summary: The even-toed hoofed mammals on land, from the rabbit-sized Eocene Diacodexis to giraffes and bison.

nodes.name: Whales, dolphins and porpoises
nodes.summary: Mammals that returned to the sea; Pakicetus and Himalayacetus from Eocene Pakistan and India, about 53-50 million years old, were wolf-sized waders with whale ears.

nodes.name: Horses, rhinos and tapirs
nodes.summary: Odd-toed hoofed mammals; Sifrhippus, a dog-sized horse of 56 million years ago, opens a famously complete fossil record.

nodes.name: Rodents, rabbits and primates
nodes.summary: The placental supergroup uniting rodents and rabbits with tree shrews, colugos and primates, which includes humans.

nodes.name: Rodents
nodes.summary: Gnawing mammals with ever-growing incisors, about 40 percent of all mammal species; Tribosphenomys and Paramys from the earliest Eocene are the first.

nodes.name: Rabbits, hares and pikas
nodes.summary: Double-incisored relatives of rodents; Eocene fossils from Asia such as Gomphos record their origin.

nodes.name: Primates
nodes.summary: Grasping-handed, forward-eyed mammals of the trees; Purgatorius from the earliest Paleocene (66 million years) may be the first, and true primates such as Teilhardina appear at 56 million years.

nodes.name: Lemurs and lorises
nodes.summary: Wet-nosed primates, today mainly the lemurs of Madagascar and the lorises and galagos of Africa and Asia.

nodes.name: Monkeys and apes
nodes.summary: The anthropoid primates; Eosimias from the Eocene of China, about 45 million years old, is among the earliest.

nodes.name: New World monkeys
nodes.summary: Monkeys of the Americas, many with prehensile tails, descended from African ancestors that crossed the Atlantic; Perupithecus from Peru, about 36 million years old, is the oldest.

nodes.name: Old World monkeys and apes
nodes.summary: Downward-nosed primates of Africa and Asia; the monkey and ape lines diverged about 25-30 million years ago.

nodes.name: Old World monkeys
nodes.summary: Baboons, macaques, colobus monkeys and langurs; Victoriapithecus from Kenya records the group at about 19 million years.

nodes.name: Apes
nodes.summary: Tailless primates: gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and humans; Rukwapithecus and Proconsul from East Africa open the record about 25-21 million years ago.

nodes.name: Humans and chimpanzees
nodes.summary: The human and chimpanzee lineages parted about 6-9 million years ago; Sahelanthropus from Chad, around 7 million years old, may stand near the split.

nodes.name: Chimpanzees and bonobos
nodes.summary: Our closest living relatives, sharing about 98.8 percent of our DNA; the two species separated about one to two million years ago when the Congo River formed a barrier.

nodes.name: Australopithecines
nodes.summary: Small-brained upright walkers of Africa such as 'Lucy' (Au. afarensis, 3.2 million years); the genus spans about 4.2 to 2 million years ago and gave rise to Homo.

nodes.name: Humans (genus Homo)
nodes.summary: Larger-brained, tool-making hominins; a jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, dated to 2.8 million years, is the oldest fossil assigned to the genus.

nodes.name: Homo erectus
nodes.summary: The first hominin to leave Africa and to control fire, with a body plan much like ours; it persisted in Java until about 110,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Neanderthals
nodes.summary: Stocky, large-brained humans of Ice Age Europe and western Asia who made tools, fire and ornaments; they disappeared about 40,000 years ago but live on in a few percent of most people's genomes.

nodes.name: Modern humans
nodes.summary: Our own species; skulls from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, dated to about 315,000 years, are the oldest fossils with modern human features, and all living people descend from African populations.

nodes.name: Reptiles (including birds)
nodes.summary: The amniote branch leading to all living reptiles and birds; Hylonomus from the Late Carboniferous of Nova Scotia is the oldest.

nodes.name: Parareptiles
nodes.summary: An early reptile radiation including the cow-sized pareiasaurs and the lizard-like procolophonids; the last of them died at the end of the Triassic.

nodes.name: Diapsids
nodes.summary: Reptiles with two openings behind each eye: lizards, snakes, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds; Petrolacosaurus from Kansas, about 302 million years old, is the earliest.

nodes.name: Ichthyosaurs
nodes.summary: Dolphin-shaped marine reptiles that gave birth at sea; they appeared right after the end-Permian extinction and died out in the Late Cretaceous, about 94 million years ago.

nodes.name: Plesiosaurs and relatives
nodes.summary: Marine reptiles from the Triassic nothosaurs and placodonts to the long-necked plesiosaurs and big-headed pliosaurs, which lasted until the end of the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Lepidosaurs
nodes.summary: Scaly reptiles that shed their skin: the tuatara and the lizards and snakes; Megachirella from the Middle Triassic shows the group was established by 240 million years ago.

nodes.name: Tuatara
nodes.summary: A once-widespread Mesozoic group now reduced to a single species on New Zealand islands, the tuatara, with a lineage reaching back to the Triassic.

nodes.name: Lizards and snakes
nodes.summary: The most diverse living reptiles, over 11,000 species; Megachirella wachtleri from the Italian Alps, 240 million years old, is the oldest known squamate.

nodes.name: Mosasaurs
nodes.summary: Lizards that became the top marine predators of the Late Cretaceous, some over 15 metres long; they vanished in the end-Cretaceous extinction.

nodes.name: Snakes
nodes.summary: Legless lizards with flexible jaws; Eophis from the Middle Jurassic of England, about 167 million years old, is the oldest snake, and four-legged early snakes persisted into the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Turtles, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds
nodes.summary: Genomes place turtles as the closest relatives of the archosaurs (crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds), together forming Archelosauria.

nodes.name: Turtles and tortoises
nodes.summary: Reptiles encased in a shell grown from ribs and vertebrae; Pappochelys (240 million years) and the half-shelled Odontochelys (220 million years) record how the shell was assembled.

nodes.name: Archosaurs
nodes.summary: The 'ruling reptiles' that rose after the end-Permian extinction and split, within a few million years, into the crocodile line and the bird line.

nodes.name: Crocodilians and relatives
nodes.summary: The crocodile line of archosaurs, which produced armoured aetosaurs and running rauisuchians in the Triassic and today survives as 27 species of crocodiles, alligators and gharials.

nodes.name: Bird-line archosaurs
nodes.summary: The archosaur branch with ankle joints suited to upright walking: pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds.

nodes.name: Pterosaurs
nodes.summary: The first flying vertebrates, with wings of skin stretched from an elongated fourth finger; from sparrow-sized forms to the ten-metre-wingspan Quetzalcoatlus, all died 66 million years ago.

nodes.name: Dinosaurs
nodes.summary: Upright-walking archosaurs that ruled the land for 165 million years; Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus from Argentina (about 231 million years) are among the first, and Nyasasaurus may push the origin to 243 million years.

nodes.name: Bird-hipped dinosaurs (Triceratops, Stegosaurus)
nodes.summary: Plant-eating dinosaurs with backward-pointing pubic bones: horned ceratopsians, armoured ankylosaurs, plated stegosaurs and duck-billed hadrosaurs, all lost at the end of the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Long-necked dinosaurs (Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus)
nodes.summary: From the small Triassic Eoraptor-grade forms to the largest land animals ever, 30-metre sauropods weighing over 50 tonnes; the lineage ended with the Cretaceous.

nodes.name: Theropods
nodes.summary: Mostly meat-eating, two-legged dinosaurs with hollow bones and, in many, feathers; birds are living theropods.

nodes.name: Non-avian theropods (Tyrannosaurus, Velociraptor)
nodes.summary: The predatory dinosaurs from Coelophysis to Tyrannosaurus and the feathered dromaeosaurs; every line except the birds died in the end-Cretaceous extinction.

nodes.name: Birds
nodes.summary: Feathered, flying theropods; Archaeopteryx from the Late Jurassic of Germany, about 150 million years old, remains the oldest widely accepted bird, with feathered relatives such as Anchiornis slightly older.

nodes.name: Ostriches, emus, kiwi and tinamous
nodes.summary: Birds with an ancient palate structure, mostly flightless giants whose flightlessness evolved several times; their split from all other living birds is a Late Cretaceous clock estimate.

nodes.name: Fowl: chickens, ducks and geese
nodes.summary: Landfowl and waterfowl; Asteriornis from Belgium, 66.7 million years old, and Vegavis from Antarctica are the oldest modern-type birds and sit on this branch.

nodes.name: Neoaves (most living birds)
nodes.summary: About 95 percent of living bird species, from hummingbirds and penguins to eagles and parrots, which radiated explosively in the few million years after the end-Cretaceous extinction.

nodes.name: Perching birds and songbirds
nodes.summary: More than half of all bird species, with a foot built for perching; molecular clocks place their origin in the Eocene, and the oldest fossils are about 55-50 million years old.
